title: The Perfect Courtier
summary: To survive and thrive in the court of power, one must master the arts of the perfect courtier. This involves playing to the master's ego, making difficult tasks look effortless, adapting your style and body language to those you deal with, and bringing only good news. A courtier must avoid bragging, refrain from direct criticism, ask for favors sparingly, and never mock a superior's appearance or taste. Mastering self-control, hiding deceptive deeds, and becoming a source of pleasure are essential to securing power and staying in favor.
example: Alexander the Great's companion was beheaded for being too honest and offering bitter criticism.
Han Dynasty courtiers used fictional historical scenarios to subtly guide and warn their kings without facing execution.
A French architect at Versailles secured his position by planting minor mistakes in his plans to let the king find and correct them, flattering the king's ego.
A fashion expert fell into poverty after joking about a prince's appearance.
An employee who covered a drunken, sleeping king with his coat was executed for exceeding his assigned duties and making the master look incompetent.
A painter voluntarily degraded the quality of his own work to avoid provoking the envy and resentment of a colleague.
reversal: There is no real reversal for this law, as disobeying its rules brings no benefits.
If you do cross the line or deceive your master, you must hide it completely and use clever manipulation to restore their trust, as Talleyrand did with Napoleon.
